This Week in Democracy: Los Angeles Becomes the Test Case

Immigration raids, a federalized National Guard, a senator in handcuffs, and a nationwide day of protest

```markdown This week, Los Angeles became the place where the country's arguments about immigration enforcement, federal power, and dissent stopped being abstract. What began as a series of workplace raids grew, over six days, into a National Guard deployment fought out in federal court, a sitting senator forced to the ground in handcuffs, and finally the largest coordinated day of protest of the term. The throughline connecting these moments was not accident but escalation: each step built on the one before it, and each drew a response that raised the stakes further.

The pattern started over the weekend. Department of Homeland Security agents conducted coordinated raids across Los Angeles workplaces, including a Home Depot and a clothing manufacturer, arresting at least 45 people without warrants. Agents used flash-bang grenades and military-style tactics; among those detained was the president of SEIU California. Governor Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass condemned the operation immediately, setting up a conflict between federal enforcement priorities and local government that would define the rest of the week. The administration moved on several other fronts at once: a ban on entry from twelve countries, suspension of Harvard's student visa program, rescission of emergency abortion guidance, a filing to resume mass federal firings, and new investigations into Joe Biden's pardons and mental competency. Federal judges pushed back almost immediately, blocking deportations under the Alien Enemies Act, blocking cuts to gender-affirming care in federal prisons, and stopping the elimination of Job Corps. But even as courts intervened, a more basic form of oversight failed: Representatives Jimmy Gomez, Luz Rivas, Norma Torres, and Lou Correa were turned away from federal detention facilities in Los Angeles despite holding statutory authority to inspect them, with reports that detainees lacked access to food, water, and medicine.

By Monday, the numbers themselves became the story. ICE detained more than 2,200 people in a single day, the largest daily total in the agency's history, after deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller reportedly demanded a minimum of 3,000 arrests per day and warned of firings if the pace didn't increase — enforcement driven by a political target rather than individualized case review. The same day, President Trump directed cabinet members to "liberate" Los Angeles from what he called a migrant invasion, casting protests against the raids as violent riots against federal law enforcement, a characterization the Los Angeles Police Department's own public statements did not support. That framing would become the rationale for federalizing the state's National Guard. Congressional access problems recurred, with Democratic members again denied entry to detention facilities in both Los Angeles and New York. Separately, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard was accused by senior Democrats of "illegal interference" after firing the acting counsel to the intelligence community's inspector general, raising concerns about the independence of internal watchdogs. And journalists covering the Los Angeles protests, including CNN's Jason Carroll and Australian reporter Lauren Tomasi, were struck by rubber bullets or briefly detained, prompting a coalition letter warning of First Amendment violations.

Tuesday was the week's densest day for institutional pressure. California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Governor Newsom filed suit against the federalization of the state's National Guard, arguing it violated the Tenth Amendment and state sovereignty — a case that would move with unusual speed over the following days. On the public health front, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. dismissed all seventeen members of the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices in what he called a "clean sweep," replacing an independent scientific panel with appointees answerable directly to him. At Fort Bragg, Trump announced plans to restore Confederate-derived names to Army installations, reversing a bipartisan congressional decision. Pressure on institutions perceived as adversarial broadened considerably: the administration threatened school funding over lessons on systemic racism, escalated its dispute with Harvard over admissions and hiring, banned federal grants that used "gender ideology" terminology, threatened university funding over allowing protests, pulled American Bar Association grants after the group's criticism of the administration, and moved to defund NPR and PBS while continuing to retaliate against the Associated Press. The State Department revoked roughly 800 student visas tied largely to pro-Palestine protest activity, and USCIS announced plans to monitor immigrants' social media for "antisemitic activity." Even symbolic space came under scrutiny, as the Department of Defense ordered nearly 400 books removed from the Naval Academy library and banned pride flags from State Department and VA offices.

Wednesday offered a partial check and a grim illustration of enforcement's reach. A federal judge ruled that the administration could not detain Columbia activist Mahmoud Khalil on the theory that his presence posed foreign policy consequences, though a separate immigration charge kept him in custody — a narrow but real limit on a novel executive theory for detaining noncitizens over political speech. Meanwhile, ICE raids disrupted essential labor: about 75 workers were detained at a Nebraska meatpacking plant, and raids hit produce farms in Ventura County, California, unsettling immigrant workforces central to the food supply. Governor Newsom delivered a prime-time address condemning both the raids and the National Guard federalization, urging peaceful protest while warning against the erosion of civil liberties. And in Downey, California, unidentified federal agents detained a man outside a church, with one agent pointing a rifle at a pastor who tried to intervene — a small, sharp episode that crystallized concerns about accountability among unidentified enforcement personnel operating in civilian spaces.

Thursday produced the week's starkest images. California Senator Alex Padilla, a ranking member of the Senate's immigration subcommittee, was forced to the ground and handcuffed by federal agents after attempting to ask Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem a question during a press conference on the Los Angeles operations. He was released without charge, but the incident — a sitting senator physically restrained while attempting oversight — drew immediate bipartisan condemnation and became one of the week's defining moments. Hours earlier, in a legal sense, the week's central constitutional question had reached a verdict: Judge Charles Breyer ruled that Trump's federalization of the California National Guard exceeded his statutory authority and violated the Tenth Amendment, ordering control returned to Governor Newsom. The victory was short-lived. Within hours, the Ninth Circuit issued an administrative stay, keeping the troops under federal control pending a hearing set for June 17 — a sequence that showed how quickly a district court check on executive power could be blunted by appellate procedure rather than resolved on the merits. The same day, Trump signed congressional resolutions overturning California's ban on new gas-powered car sales by 2035 and its truck emissions rules, prompting a new multistate lawsuit, while his earlier takeover of the Kennedy Center continued to generate falling ticket sales and performer cancellations. Ahead of planned nationwide demonstrations, governors and law enforcement officials in Texas, Missouri, South Carolina, Virginia, and Florida announced National Guard call-ups or zero-tolerance postures, and a Florida sheriff issued a widely criticized threat of lethal force against protesters. House Republicans, meanwhile, narrowly passed a $9.4 billion rescissions package defunding NPR and PBS, sending it to the Senate.

Friday brought the week to its intended culmination, on more than one front. A federal judge in Massachusetts issued an injunction against parts of Trump's executive order requiring proof of citizenship to vote and penalizing states over ballot deadlines, finding a "substantial risk" of voter disenfranchisement — the second such ruling after an earlier one from a judge in Washington, D.C. In New Jersey, the Justice Department indicted Representative LaMonica McIver on three counts of impeding federal officers during a protest and oversight visit to an ICE detention center in Newark; McIver called the charges political intimidation. Taken together with Padilla's removal two days earlier, the indictment meant that within the same week, one member of Congress had been handcuffed by federal agents and another criminally charged, both in connection with attempts to conduct oversight of immigration enforcement. Quieter but consequential actions moved alongside these headlines: the administration transferred personal data, including immigration status, for millions of Medicaid enrollees to DHS to support deportation efforts, and the EEOC's acting chair ordered a halt to processing gender-identity discrimination claims. Trump himself acknowledged that immigration enforcement was removing long-term agricultural workers and hurting farmers, an unusual admission of friction within his own administration's agenda.

And then, on Friday, the week's accumulated pressure found its expression in the streets. Organizers mobilized "No Kings" demonstrations across roughly 2,000 sites nationwide, explicitly framed as a response to the preceding days' raids, deportations, and confrontations, and to a military parade Trump had scheduled the same weekend. Millions were expected to participate across all fifty states, making it one of the largest single-day displays of coordinated public dissent of the term.

By the end of the week, no single institution had settled the underlying conflict. Courts had repeatedly found parts of the administration's immigration and election actions unlawful, only to see some of those rulings paused on appeal within hours. Congress had twice been physically or legally denied the oversight access its members are entitled to by law, and two of its elected members had been handcuffed or indicted in the course of trying to exercise that access. Local and state officials in California asserted authority over their own National Guard and environmental policy, only to have both contested or overridden by federal action within days. What the week made visible, more than any one ruling or statement, was how enforcement power, oversight power, and protest power were all being tested against one another in real time — with Los Angeles as the proving ground and the Friday demonstrations as the clearest public answer the country had yet given. ```
